title: Cache eviction heuristics prototype retro — 2026-12-07
content:
Date: 2026-12-07
Attendees: Aisha K., Marco S., Priya R., Lena O., Sam B. (observability)
Duration: 45m
Context:
- This retro covers the three-week prototype of alternate cache eviction heuristics for the KV cache component. The prototype focused on two primary ideas: 1) leaky-bucket age-weighted eviction with stochastic TTLs, and 2) a lightweight sampler that biases eviction decisions away from recently served hot prefixes. The goal was to reduce tail latency regressions under skewed traffic while keeping memory pressure and CPU overhead acceptable.

Goals for prototype:
- Reduce p99 generation latency regressions observed in earlier runs when hot-key churn spikes.
- Improve overall cache hit-rate for typical chat workloads with conversational prefixes.
- Keep additional CPU below ~3% on runtime worker process and no more than 8% extra host mem overhead.

What we ran
- Cluster: staging-inference-fleet-4 (8x A10G-like nodes)
- Workloads: mix of replayed traffic from Sept-Nov prod traces (3 traffic profiles: steady-chat, bursty-qa, system-tests with synthetic hot keys)
- Variants:
  * baseline: current LRU-with-prefill (master)
  * variant-A: leaky-bucket age-weighted eviction + stochastic TTL (PR#3421)
  * variant-B: heap-sampler + hot-key spill mitigation (sampling prob tuned to 0.12)
  * variant-C: hybrid (A then B fallback under >75% cache occupancy)
- Run length: each variant ran 8 hours per profile, 2 cold restarts between runs to clear artifacts.

Key metrics tracked
- cache_hit_rate (per-prefix and global)
- p50/p95/p99 generation latency (ms)
- CPU% of runtime worker and host
- free_cache_memory and eviction_rate
- observed hot-key amplification (requests/sec for top-100 prefixes)

Results summary (high level)
- variant-A:
  * global hit-rate: +3.1% vs baseline on steady-chat; +1.6% on bursty-qa
  * p99 latency: -12% on steady-chat, no measurable change on bursty-qa
  * CPU overhead: +1.7% on runtime worker (acceptable)
  * downside: occasional micro-stalls when eviction decisions coincided with large batch flushes (investigate race with batch-allocator)
- variant-B: 
  * global hit-rate: +0.9% on steady-chat; +4.2% on bursty-qa (better under high skew)
  * p99 latency: -18% on bursty-qa, +2% (worse) on steady-chat due to sampler noise
  * CPU overhead: +2.9% (higher)
  * memory footprint: +4% measured heap used for sampler structures
- variant-C: 
  * combined advantages: p99 down -14% across profiles, hit-rate +3.6% overall
  * complexity: slightly more state machines in eviction path, code complexity increased (harder to reason in hot path)

Observations / deeper analysis
- Batch alignment issue: when eviction ran concurrently with batch allocation spikes, we saw brief CPU stalls and an uptick in tail latency. Root cause likely lock contention inside the small allocation slab used by the evictor.
- Hot-key spillover: variant-B reduced repeated eviction/repop cycles for the single biggest hot prefixes, which matters under sustained amplification (e.g., monitoring alerts or live demos).
- Prefill interplay: eviction that prioritized age over recency favors retaining prefills that are cheap to serve. This helped steady-chat but penalized bursty-qa where recency matters more.
- Telemetry: need to capture per-eviction decision traces (sampled) to better understand misfires — added an observability ticket.

Decisions made in retro
- Short term (next sprint): ship variant-A as an opt-in config flag behind a runtime feature-gate for Dedicated customers. Rationale: improves steady-chat and has the lowest CPU cost.
- Medium term: iterate on hybrid (variant-C) but simplify control flow to avoid hot path branching; target for sprint+3.
- Do not ship variant-B to default yet due to CPU/memory overhead and unstable steady-chat behavior; keep experiment branch for further tuning.

Risks and mitigations
- Risk: micro-stalls due to allocator contention could surface under heavier production load. Mitigation: swap to per-worker evictor thread (isolates allocation) or use try-lock fast-fail path. Prioritize tests in perf lab.
- Risk: config complexity may confuse customers. Mitigation: default to baseline for hosted API and expose as advanced toggle on Dedicated. Include clear doc + examples.

Action items (owner — due)
- Marco S. — 2026-12-14: open follow-up PR to replace single global eviction lock with try-lock fast-fail and add microbench harness. Link in ticket.
- Priya R. — 2026-12-11: add sampled per-eviction traces to tracing pipeline (0.1% sample) and a dashboard for misfires.
- Lena O. — 2026-12-21: prototype simplified hybrid flow (variant-C-lite) that avoids branching in the hot path; measure CPU.
- Sam B. — 2026-12-10: create observability board with run-by-run comparisons and attach histograms for p99 shifts.
- Aisha K. — 2026-12-15: draft customer-facing docs for Dedicated opt-in flag including recommended heuristics and how to toggle safely.

Open questions
- What is the right default sampling probability for variant-B-ish approaches across regions with different traffic shapes? (Need more cross-region traces.)
- Should we expose TTL as absolute or relative to last-access time for user-configurability? (Ops/deploy implications.)

Notes / miscellaneous
- PR references: PR#3421 contains the bulk of variant-A changes; PR#3448 contains profiler scaffolding.
- Observed an unrelated 1% increase in GC cycles on one node during runs; likely test noise but flagged to infra.
- Follow-up dry-run planned in perf lab on 2026-12-13 with full-production load simulation.

Appendix: micro-bench notes (short)
- Local microbench (x4 worker process, synthetic small-prefix workload): variant-A reduced eviction churn by ~22% and improved single-worker p95 by 9%.
- Code pointers: evictor core at runtime/evictor/*.cpp, sampler at runtime/sampler/*.rs

If you have questions or want the raw traces, ping me or check the linked artifacts.
